nameStory: Few-flower Spikerush gets its name from the tiny, dark spikelet at the top of each stem that contains only 2-7 individual flowers - much fewer than most of its spikerush cousins. The 'spike' part refers to the compact, elongated cluster of flowers, while 'rush' comes from the plant's thin, upright stems that resemble true rushes, even though it's actually a sedge!
description: Few-flower Spikerush is a small, slender wetland sedge that looks like tiny green spears poking up from marshy ground. Growing up to about 16 inches tall, it has thin, flattened stems topped with small, dark brown to blackish flower spikes that are less than half an inch long. The stems are surrounded by papery, reddish-brown to green sheaths at the base, and the whole plant spreads slowly underground through creeping roots called rhizomes. Despite being called a 'rush,' it's actually a member of the sedge family.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, lance-shaped to oval dark spikelet at stem tip, less than half an inch long, containing only 2-7 individual flowers covered by brown or black bracts

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Thin, flattened stems up to 16 inches tall growing in small clusters from underground rhizomes in wet areas

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Papery, reddish-brown to green sheaths wrapped around the base of stems rather than typical blade-like leaves

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small yellow-brown achenes (dry, one-seeded fruits) about 1/8 inch long that develop after flowering

habitat: Look for Few-flower Spikerush in wet meadows, bogs, marshy areas, and along the edges of ponds or streams where the soil stays consistently moist. It thrives in calcium-rich wetlands and can occasionally be found near natural hot springs or other mineral-rich water sources. This plant prefers full sun to partial shade in areas that experience seasonal flooding or constant moisture.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from rhizomes as wetlands warm up, with thin stems beginning to elongate.
seasonality.summer: Dark flower spikelets appear at stem tips, making this the best time for positive identification of the few-flowered clusters.
seasonality.fall: Yellow-brown seed heads mature and stems begin to brown, though some may persist into early winter.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground parts die back, leaving only underground rhizomes to survive until spring regrowth.

funFact: Few-flower Spikerush is one of the most widely distributed plants on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica and Australia, yet it's so uncommon in New England that it's been observed only twice by naturalists - making it rarer here than some orchids!
confusionNotes: With 19 different spikerush species in New England, telling them apart can be tricky! The key memory trick is right in the name - count the flowers in the spikelet, and if you can only count 2-7 individual flower bracts (not 20+ like most spikerushes), you've likely found Few-flower Spikerush. Most other spikerushes have much denser, more crowded flower heads.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'rush' fool you - spikerushes are actually sedges, not true rushes. The confusion comes from their similar appearance and wetland habitat. Remember the old botanist's rhyme: 'Sedges have edges' - if you roll the stem between your fingers, sedges feel triangular or flattened, while true rushes are round.
compareHints: Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers. It's also generally smaller and more delicate than robust species like Squarestem Spikerush, and unlike some aquatic species like Needle Spikerush, it typically grows in wet soil rather than standing water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes.
Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments.
Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
